header:
How to open and
fund a Roth IRA

lines.text: Your Roth IRA can sit uninvested for years.
lines.say: Your Roth IRA can sit uninvested for years.

lines.text: Opening and funding the account isn't enough. You have to pick investments, and that's the step people miss.
lines.say: Opening and funding the account isn't enough. You have to pick investments, and that's the step people miss.

lines.text: And plenty of people never get that far. In mid-2025, about 28% of US households owned a Roth IRA.
lines.say: And plenty of people never even get that far. In mid twenty twenty-five, only about twenty-eight percent of US households owned a Roth IRA.

scene.label: US households with a Roth IRA, mid-2025
scene.sub: ICI, Role of IRAs in US Households, 2025

lines.text: And only 17% of all households put money into any IRA for 2024.
lines.say: And only seventeen percent of all households put money into any IRA for twenty twenty-four.

scene.label: Households that contributed to an IRA, tax year 2024

lines.text: So here's the whole thing, in order: check you qualify, open the account, fund it, and invest it.
lines.say: So here's the whole thing, in order: check that you qualify, open the account, fund it, and actually invest it.

lines.text: Every rule and limit here is for tax year 2026, with exact math, and the mistakes that cost people money.
lines.say: Every rule and limit here is for tax year twenty twenty-six, with the exact math, plus the mistakes that quietly cost people money.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What a Roth IRA is.
lines.say: Chapter one: what a Roth IRA actually is.

lines.text: IRA stands for individual retirement arrangement. It's an account with tax rules, not an investment by itself.
lines.say: I R A stands for individual retirement arrangement. It's an account with special tax rules, not an investment by itself.

lines.text: Think of it as a box. What you put inside the box is a separate choice.
lines.say: Think of it as a box. What you put inside the box is a completely separate choice.

lines.text: With a Roth, you pay tax now: contributions go in with money that's already been taxed. No deduction.
lines.say: With a Roth, you pay the tax now. Contributions go in with money that's already been taxed, and there's no deduction.

lines.text: The payoff comes later. Qualified withdrawals, growth included, come out tax-free.
lines.say: The payoff comes later. Qualified withdrawals, growth included, come out completely tax-free.

lines.text: Qualified usually means two things: you're at least 59½, and it's been 5 years since your first Roth tax year.
lines.say: Qualified usually means two things: you're at least fifty-nine and a half, and it's been five years since your first Roth tax year.

lines.text: The 5-year clock starts January 1 of the first tax year you contribute for. Even a 2026 contribution made in early 2027 counts as 2026.
lines.say: That five-year clock starts on January first of the first tax year you contribute for. Even a twenty twenty-six contribution made in early twenty twenty-seven counts as twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: There's also a flexible part: your own contributions can come back out any time, with no tax and no penalty.
lines.say: There's also a flexible part. Your own contributions can come back out any time, with no tax and no penalty.

lines.text: It's the earnings that have rules. Pull them early, and they can face income tax plus a 10% additional tax.
lines.say: It's the earnings that have rules. Pull those out early, and they can face income tax plus a ten percent additional tax.

lines.text: Withdrawals count your contributions first, so your earnings are the last money out.
lines.say: Withdrawals count your contributions first, so your earnings are the last money to come out.

lines.text: And there are no required withdrawals for the original owner. The money can keep growing as long as you live.
lines.say: And there are no required withdrawals for the original owner, so the money can keep growing for as long as you live.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Can you contribute?
lines.say: Chapter two: can you contribute?

lines.text: Step one is checking you qualify.
lines.say: Step one is checking that you qualify.

lines.text: Rule one: you need earned income, like wages or self-employment income. Investment income doesn't count.
lines.say: Rule one: you need earned income, like wages or self-employment income. Investment income doesn't count.

lines.text: You can't put in more than you earned. Earn $4,000 in a year, and $4,000 is your cap.
lines.say: And you can't put in more than you earned. Earn four thousand dollars in a year, and four thousand is your cap.

lines.text: One exception: a working spouse can fund an IRA for a spouse with no income, if you file jointly.
lines.say: One exception: a working spouse can fund an IRA for a spouse with no income, as long as you file jointly.

lines.text: Rule two: the dollar limit. For 2026, it's $7,500.
lines.say: Rule two is the dollar limit. For twenty twenty-six, it's seventy-five hundred dollars.

lines.text: Age 50 or older? Add a $1,100 catch-up, for $8,600.
lines.say: If you're fifty or older, you can add an eleven hundred dollar catch-up, for eighty-six hundred total.

lines.text: That limit has risen over time, first by law, then with inflation. Back in 2002, it was $3,000.
lines.say: That limit has risen over time, first by law, then with inflation. Back in two thousand two, it was three thousand dollars.

lines.text: The 2026 limit is 2.5 times what it was in 2002.
lines.say: The twenty twenty-six limit is two and a half times what it was in two thousand two.

lines.text: Important: the limit is shared. Traditional and Roth IRAs together can't go over $7,500.
lines.say: Here's the important part: the limit is shared. Your traditional and Roth IRAs together can't go over seventy-five hundred.

lines.text: Your 401(k) at work has its own separate limit, so it doesn't use up your IRA room.
lines.say: Your four oh one K at work has its own separate limit, so it doesn't use up your IRA room.

lines.text: Rule three is income. Roth IRAs phase out for higher earners, based on modified adjusted gross income.
lines.say: Rule three is income. Roth IRAs phase out for higher earners, based on something called modified adjusted gross income.

lines.text: For 2026, single and head-of-household filers phase out between $153,000 and $168,000.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-six, single and head-of-household filers phase out between a hundred fifty-three thousand and a hundred sixty-eight thousand dollars.

lines.text: Married couples filing jointly phase out between $242,000 and $252,000.
lines.say: Married couples filing jointly phase out between two hundred forty-two thousand and two hundred fifty-two thousand.

lines.text: Below the range, you get the full amount. Above it, you can't contribute directly at all.
lines.say: Below the range, you get the full amount. Above it, you can't contribute directly at all.

lines.text: Inside the range, you get a partial amount. Let's do the math for a single filer with a MAGI of $160,500.
lines.say: Inside the range, you get a partial amount. Let's do the math for a single filer with a MAGI of a hundred sixty thousand five hundred.

lines.text: They're $7,500 into a $15,000-wide range. That's halfway, so the limit is cut in half.
lines.say: They're seventy-five hundred dollars into a fifteen-thousand-dollar range. That's exactly halfway, so the limit gets cut in half.

lines.text: Half of $7,500 is $3,750. That's their Roth limit for 2026.
lines.say: Half of seventy-five hundred is thirty-seven fifty. That's their Roth limit for twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: The IRS rounds the result up to the next $10, and if it's above zero, you can always put in at least $200.
lines.say: The I R S rounds the result up to the next ten dollars, and if it's above zero, you can always put in at least two hundred.

lines.text: Income too high? Some people use a backdoor Roth: a traditional IRA contribution, then a conversion.
lines.say: Income too high? Some people use what's called a backdoor Roth: a traditional IRA contribution, then a conversion to Roth.

lines.text: Careful, though: if you hold other pre-tax IRA money, the pro-rata rule can make part of a conversion taxable.
lines.say: Careful, though. If you already hold other pre-tax IRA money, the pro-rata rule can make part of that conversion taxable.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Open the account.
lines.say: Chapter three: open the account.

lines.text: Step two is opening it, which usually takes a few minutes online.
lines.say: Step two is opening it, which usually takes just a few minutes online.

lines.text: You open a Roth IRA with a provider. The common types are brokerages, robo-advisors, banks and credit unions.
lines.say: You open a Roth IRA with a provider. The common types are brokerages, robo-advisors, and banks or credit unions.

lines.text: A brokerage lets you pick your own funds and stocks.
lines.say: A brokerage lets you pick your own funds and stocks.

lines.text: A robo-advisor picks a mix for you based on a questionnaire, usually for an annual fee.
lines.say: A robo-advisor picks a mix for you based on a short questionnaire, usually for an annual fee.

scene.label: auto mix
scene.caption: Robo-advisor: invests for you, for a fee
scene.name: ROBO-ADVISOR

lines.text: A bank IRA often holds savings or CDs: steady, but with a narrower menu.
lines.say: A bank I R A often holds savings or C Ds, which is steady, but comes with a much narrower menu.

lines.text: Whichever you look at, compare the same things: fees, the investment menu, and any account minimums.
lines.say: Whichever type you look at, compare the same three things: fees, the investment menu, and any account minimums.

lines.text: Fees matter because they come out every year, whether your investments go up or down.
lines.say: Fees matter because they come out every year, whether your investments go up or down.

lines.text: To apply, have your Social Security number, ID, address, employer info and a bank account for transfers.
lines.say: To apply, have your Social Security number, an ID, your address, your employer's info, and a bank account for transfers.

lines.text: Make sure you pick Roth IRA on the form, not traditional. It's one click, and it matters.
lines.say: Make sure you pick Roth I R A on the form, not traditional. It's one click, and it really matters.

lines.text: Then name a beneficiary, the person who inherits the account. It's easy to skip and painful to miss.
lines.say: Then name a beneficiary, the person who inherits the account. It's easy to skip, and painful to miss.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Fund it.
lines.say: Chapter four: fund it.

lines.text: Step three is getting money in.
lines.say: Step three is getting money in.

lines.text: Link your bank account, then make a one-time transfer, set up automatic deposits, or both.
lines.say: Link your bank account, then make a one-time transfer, set up automatic deposits, or do both.

lines.text: Here's the math on a $7,500 limit: spread over 12 months, it's $625 a month.
lines.say: Here's the math on a seventy-five hundred dollar limit. Spread over twelve months, it's six hundred twenty-five dollars a month.

lines.text: Paid every two weeks? Over 26 paychecks, it's $288.46 each.
lines.say: If you're paid every two weeks, that's twenty-six paychecks, or about two hundred eighty-eight dollars each.

lines.text: Or $144.23 a week. Any amount counts, though. You don't have to max it out.
lines.say: Or about a hundred forty-four dollars a week. Any amount counts, though. You don't have to max it out.

lines.text: Now the deadline. You can contribute for a tax year until that year's tax filing deadline.
lines.say: Now, the deadline. You can contribute for a tax year right up until that year's tax filing deadline.

lines.text: So 2026 contributions are allowed until April 15, 2027, which still leaves time to fund 2026. Extensions don't count.
lines.say: So contributions for twenty twenty-six are allowed until April fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven, which still leaves time to fund twenty twenty-six. Filing extensions don't count.

lines.text: Between January and April, tell your provider which year a deposit is for. Otherwise it may count for the current year.
lines.say: Between January and April, tell your provider which year a deposit is for, or it may count toward the current year.

lines.text: The IRS announces next year's limits each fall. Check IRS.gov for the 2027 numbers.
lines.say: The I R S announces next year's limits each fall, so check I R S dot gov for the twenty twenty-seven numbers.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Invest it.
lines.say: Chapter five: invest it.

lines.text: Step four is the one people miss.
lines.say: Step four is the one people miss.

lines.text: When money lands in your IRA, it usually sits in a cash or money market position first.
lines.say: When money lands in your I R A, it usually sits in a cash or money market position first.

lines.text: It may earn a little interest, but it isn't in the investments you had in mind until you place an order.
lines.say: It may earn a little interest, but it isn't in the investments you had in mind until you actually place an order.

lines.text: Robo-advisors usually invest automatically. At a brokerage, you choose.
lines.say: Robo-advisors usually invest automatically. At a brokerage, you're the one who chooses.

lines.text: Common choices include target-date funds, broad index funds, bond funds, and CDs.
lines.say: Common choices include target-date funds, broad index funds, bond funds, and C Ds.

lines.text: A target-date fund holds a mix that gets more conservative as its target year gets closer.
lines.say: A target-date fund holds a mix that gets more conservative as its target year gets closer.

lines.text: Broad index funds hold many companies at once, and many have low fees.
lines.say: Broad index funds hold lots of companies at once, and many of them have low fees.

lines.text: Bonds and CDs swing less, and usually grow less over long periods. Every option is a trade-off between risk and growth.
lines.say: Bonds and C Ds swing less, and usually grow less over long periods. Every option trades risk against growth.

lines.text: Before you pick, check each fund's expense ratio, the yearly fee as a percent of what you hold.
lines.say: Before you pick, check each fund's expense ratio, which is the yearly fee as a percent of what you hold.

lines.text: Why does investing matter so much here? Because the tax-free part is the growth.
lines.say: Why does investing matter so much here? Because the tax-free part is the growth.

lines.text: A hypothetical, not a prediction: $7,500 a year for 30 years, at a steady 7% a year.
lines.say: Here's a hypothetical, not a prediction: seventy-five hundred a year for thirty years, at a steady seven percent a year.

lines.text: You'd put in $225,000. The other $483,456 would be growth, tax-free if withdrawals are qualified.
lines.say: You'd put in two hundred twenty-five thousand. The other four hundred eighty-three thousand would be growth, tax-free if your withdrawals are qualified.

lines.text: Real returns go up and down, and can be negative. The point is the tax rule, not the number.
lines.say: Real returns go up and down, and they can be negative. The point is the tax rule, not the number.

lines.text: The same contributions left in cash would likely have grown much less, though with less risk, leaving the tax-free perk little to work with.
lines.say: The same contributions left in cash would likely have grown much less, though with less risk, leaving the tax-free perk very little to work with.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Mistakes that cost money.
lines.say: Chapter six: mistakes that cost money.

lines.text: Mistake one: putting in too much. Go over the limit, and the excess is taxed 6% for every year it stays.
lines.say: Mistake one is putting in too much. Go over the limit, and the excess is taxed six percent for every year it stays in.

lines.text: Example: $1,000 too much, left in for 2 years, costs $120 in excise tax.
lines.say: For example, a thousand dollars too much, left in for two years, costs a hundred twenty dollars in excise tax.

lines.text: The fix: take out the excess plus what it earned, by your tax filing deadline including extensions.
lines.say: The fix is to take out the excess, plus whatever it earned, by your tax filing deadline, including extensions.

lines.text: Mistake two: forgetting that a raise can push you into the phase-out. Check your MAGI before you contribute.
lines.say: Mistake two is forgetting that a raise can push you into the phase-out. Check your MAGI before you contribute.

lines.text: Mistake three: depositing and never investing. Check that the cash actually got invested.
lines.say: Mistake three is depositing and never investing. Log in and check that the cash actually got invested.

lines.text: Mistake four: pulling out earnings early. Contributions are flexible. Earnings before 59½ and 5 years usually aren't.
lines.say: Mistake four is pulling out earnings early. Contributions are flexible, but earnings before fifty-nine and a half and five years usually aren't.

lines.text: A few exceptions exist, like up to $10,000 of earnings for a first home once the 5 years are met.
lines.say: A few exceptions do exist, like up to ten thousand dollars of earnings for a first home, once the five years are met.

lines.text: Mistake five: missing the April deadline. A year you don't use is room you never get back.
lines.say: Mistake five is missing the April deadline. A year you don't use is room you never get back.

lines.text: And mistake six: picking traditional by accident, or forgetting the beneficiary. Both take a minute to check.
lines.say: And mistake six is picking traditional by accident, or forgetting the beneficiary. Both take about a minute to check.

lines.text: Recap: the one-screen checklist.
lines.say: Recap: the one-screen checklist.

lines.text: One: you need earned income, and you can't put in more than you earned.
lines.say: One: you need earned income, and you can't put in more than you earned.

lines.text: Two: stay at or below $7,500 for 2026 across all your IRAs, or $8,600 at 50 and older.
lines.say: Two: stay at or below seventy-five hundred for twenty twenty-six across all your IRAs, or eighty-six hundred at fifty and older.

lines.text: Three: check your MAGI against $153,000 to $168,000 single, or $242,000 to $252,000 joint.
lines.say: Three: check your MAGI against a hundred fifty-three to a hundred sixty-eight thousand if you're single, or two forty-two to two fifty-two if you file jointly.

lines.text: Four: after you deposit, actually invest it, and name a beneficiary.
lines.say: Four: after you deposit, actually invest it, and name a beneficiary.

lines.text: And for 2026, the last day to contribute is April 15, 2027.
lines.say: And for twenty twenty-six, the last day to contribute is April fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: A Roth IRA is a box with a great tax rule. Opening it is easy. Filling it, and investing what's inside, is the part that counts.
lines.say: A Roth IRA is a box with a great tax rule. Opening it is easy. Filling it, and investing what's inside, is the part that counts.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.yt_desc:
A step-by-step guide to opening and funding a Roth IRA for tax year 2026: who qualifies (earned income, the $7,500 limit or $8,600 at 50+, and the $153,000-$168,000 single and $242,000-$252,000 joint income phase-outs), how to open an account, how to fund it by the April 15, 2027 deadline, and why your deposit isn't invested until you pick investments. It also walks through a partial-contribution example, the 6% excess-contribution tax, withdrawal rules, and a one-screen checklist.

CHAPTERS

Sources: IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 limits); IRS Publications 590-A and 590-B; IRS historical IRA limits; ICI, The Role of IRAs in US Households' Saving for Retirement, 2025 (2026).

News and education, not financial advice.
